US Treasury futures declined as demand for havens waned on signs that the recent selloff in equities may be drawing some buyers back.
Futures on 10-year Treasury notes fell 9/32 to 106 18/32 in the early Asian session on Monday, the equivalent of a roughly four-basis-point advance. There’s no cash trading in the region due to a public holiday in Japan.

South Korean and Chinese shares fell as a global technology stock rout intensified, testing Asian authorities’ efforts to restore investor confidence as the AI trade unraveled.
The benchmark Kospi Index dropped as much as 4.4%, following Friday’s losses on Wall Street that sent the S&P 500 into a technical correction and the Nasdaq 100 posting its worst week since March 2020. Korea has trimmed the year’s rally, which at one point reached more than 110%, to just 10%.

US equity-index futures rallied as buyers returned following Friday’s selloff, which was sparked by an unwinding of the artificial intelligence trade. Treasury futures fell and the yen weakened as demand for haven assets ebbed.
Contracts for the S&P 500 Index rose 2.1% after the underlying gauge dropped for a seventh straight day Friday, entering a technical correction. Nasdaq 100 Index futures rose 2.8% as Asian trading began, following the tech-heavy gauge’s worst week in more than six years and a slide that brought it close to bear-market territory.

US stock futures rebounded as dip buyers stepped in following a steep selloff that saw a violent rotation out of technology shares, in a signal of heightened volatility in the artificial intelligence trade.
Futures on the S&P 500 traded up 2% at 7:30 p.m. in New York, while contracts on the Nasdaq 100 rose as much as 3%. That follows the Nasdaq’s worst week since 2020, and an 11% drop in a closely watched gauge of chipmakers. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average both entered a correction territory on Friday, defined as a decline of at least 10% from an all-time high.

Gold rebounded from its biggest weekly decline in eight months as traders scaled back bets on the Federal Reserve raising interest rates in the near term.
Bullion rose as much as 1.3% to around $3,582 an ounce, after falling 9% last week to a 14-month low. Traders are paring expectations of monetary tightening after growing concerns about artificial intelligence spending rippled across markets, sending technology stocks plunging.

item.title: World's Biggest Warrants Market Is Fueled by Unusual Trading in Hong Kong
item.description:
November 22, 2026 at 6:00 PM EST
Every weekday at 9:30 a.m. in Hong Kong, the world’s biggest warrants market opens with a rapid-fire burst of trading.
Huge blocks of derivative warrants and so-called callable bull/bear contracts — products that allow investors to make highly leveraged bets on stocks and other assets — zip repeatedly between accounts: one million, 5 million, 10 million, and on and on.
The activity is so intense, and so consistent, that about two-thirds of all the volume in the usual 5.5-hour trading day appears within the first 30 minutes, according to data compiled by Bloomberg for August through October. That’s extreme by almost any standard: In Germany, home to the world’s second-biggest warrants market, the figure is less than 4%. It’s 18% in Hong Kong’s cash equities market and 8% on the New York Stock Exchange, where volume is highest at the end of the trading day.
Repeated Trades Drive the Morning Rush
Share of daily trading volume in derivative warrants and CBBCs in Hong Kong, August-October
Source: Data compiled by Bloomberg
Note: Repeated trades are defined as four or more blocks of the same size in the same warrant or CBBC within any 60-second span
Few market participants in Hong Kong are willing to talk openly about the phenomenon, let alone call out the firms arranging the transactions, but in private they nearly all concur: The morning flurry has the tell-tale signs of artificially inflated trading. More than a dozen current and former traders, bankers and investors — all of whom asked not to be named discussing a sensitive subject — said these “ping pong” transactions, where issuers trade back and forth with select counterparties at minimal price changes, are meant to make certain warrants appear more in-demand than they really are.
